intuition: Build the schedule by repeatedly taking a course with no unfinished prerequisites. After taking it, lower the requirement counts of courses that depend on it. This creates a valid order directly. If the order cannot include every course, a cycle makes a full schedule impossible.

Store outgoing edges from each prerequisite to its dependents and count each course’s unfinished incoming edges. Courses with zero incoming count are ready now, including courses unrelated to any prerequisite. Processing one ready course decreases the counts of exactly its dependents.

The queue produces a valid prefix because every emitted course has already had all prerequisites emitted. A cycle can leave a remaining group in which every course still waits on another. If processing stops before all courses are emitted, no complete valid order exists; returning a partial prefix would hide that impossibility.

steps: For four courses and pairs [[1,0],[2,0],[3,1],[3,2]], create edges 0→1, 0→2, 1→3, and 2→3.
The initial indegrees are [0,1,1,2], so only course 0 enters the ready queue.
Emit 0. Decrease the counts of courses 1 and 2 to zero, adding both to the queue.
Emit 1 next. Course 3 still has indegree 1 because prerequisite 2 is unfinished, so it does not become ready yet.
Emit 2, reducing course 3’s indegree to zero. Then emit 3.
All four courses were emitted, so return [0,1,2,3]. Swapping courses 1 and 2 would also be a valid answer.

codeNotes.note: The edge follows the direction of work unlocked after completion, not the opposite textual order of the input pair.
A dependent is ready only after every incoming obligation was removed, preventing premature scheduling after just one prerequisite.

codeNotes.code: return order if len(order) == numCourses else []
codeNotes.note: A shortened order indicates blocked cyclic dependencies. Reject the incomplete schedule rather than presenting its ready prefix as a full answer.

keyDecision: Return the order only when its length equals numCourses; otherwise return an empty list.
